Most statistics teaching — and most statistics textbooks — present formulas as things to be memorised: here is the formula for variance, here is the formula for a t-statistic, learn them, apply them. This book takes a different, deliberately slower path, in the spirit of Richard Feynman’s teaching: start from what you already know and build, without a single unexplained leap. Every idea here is derived, not asserted. Before a formula is given, the specific problem it solves is explained first, so that by the time the formula appears, it feels less like something to memorise and more like the only reasonable answer to a question you already understand.

This matters more, not less, for a working clinician. An MD Community Medicine resident who has memorised “divide by n−1 for sample variance” without knowing why will apply the rule correctly on an exam and then completely fail to recognise when it doesn’t apply — a clustered dataset, an unusual missingness pattern, a test built on an assumption quietly violated. Understanding the chain of reasoning behind a technique is what lets you recognise its edges. That is the entire premise of this book: no mugging up, an unbroken chain from first principles to the techniques used in real research.
